name: Titanium dioxide sunscreen

lead: Titanium dioxide sunscreens use a mineral filter that gives good protection against UVB and part of UVA, used for slower photoaging and less sun damage. It is usually paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage.

Fine particles on the skin absorb UV light and scatter some of it. With zinc oxide it is one of the two filters the FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021. It does not fully cover the UVA range, and some products add iron oxide to block visible light.

paras: People use it in mineral sunscreens and tinted daily creams, often ultrafine versions combined with zinc oxide, applied to the face and body before sun exposure.
White cast is a common cosmetic complaint. Inhaled TiO2 dust is classified Group 2B by IARC, which is why sprays draw caution. A 1990s pilot study looked at absorption through human skin.

web.title: How to select a sunscreen - AAD
Sunscreen: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun - FDA

angle.text: Titanium dioxide sunscreens are used for mineral-based protection, strongest against UVB and partly UVA, and are often paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage. Less UV damage slows photoaging and keeps tone even.

lead: Titanium dioxide sunscreen uses titanium dioxide (TiO2), an inorganic mineral, as an ultraviolet filter. With zinc oxide it is one of the two mineral filters in sunscreens, and the two were the only filters the US FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021.[1][1]

People use it to protect the skin from sun exposure, which dermatology sources associate with photoaging, uneven pigmentation and skin cancer; keeping the skin out of UV damage is the route by which sunscreen is said to preserve a smoother, more even complexion.[1][2] Mineral products are also chosen by people who prefer a non-chemical filter, though they can leave a white cast, so formulators use ultrafine particles and tints.[1][3][1]

Wikipedia says titanium dioxide offers good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range.[1] Sunscreens use ultrafine (nanoscale) forms, often combined with ultrafine zinc oxide, and some add iron oxide to block visible light.[3][1] Published work on the ingredient includes a 1990s pilot study of absorption through human skin, a yeast-based photosafety model, and patents on mineral powder blends.[4][5][6]
infobox: FDA GRASE (2021 order); with zinc oxide the only filters so classed[1][1]
Zinc oxide approved as UV filter 2016; nanoparticle use must be labelled[1]

paras: Titanium dioxide is a white mineral pigment that is made industrially from titanium ores by the chloride or sulfate process and is produced on a scale of millions of tonnes a year for paints, plastics, paper and other uses.[3] In sunscreen it is one of the two inorganic or mineral active ingredients, the other being zinc oxide. Products built only on these two ingredients are often sold as mineral, physical or non-chemical sunscreens, in contrast to products that rely on organic (carbon-based) filters such as avobenzone or octocrylene.[1]

The FDA lists zinc oxide and titanium dioxide among the commonly used active ingredients in sunscreens, regulates sunscreens as nonprescription drugs, and advises choosing a broad-spectrum product, meaning one that protects against both UVA and UVB radiation.[7] The American Academy of Dermatology's label guidance recommends broad-spectrum protection with an SPF of 30 or higher, and water resistance for swimming or sweating; its page on choosing a sunscreen does not single out mineral filters.[2]

Wikipedia describes mineral filters as working mainly by absorbing UV, with some reflection and scattering.[1] In plastics and other materials the article on titanium dioxide attributes its UV protection to light scattering from its high refractive index, in contrast to organic filters that absorb UV.[3] Early-2000s research cited by Wikipedia suggested zinc oxide gives better protection than titanium dioxide at 340-380 nm in the UVA range, which is one reason the two are often combined.[1]

Because mineral products can leave a white cast, formulators use ultrafine particles and blends of particle sizes.[1][3][8] Larger particles may give some visible and infrared light protection but are often unacceptable to consumers for their opacity; adding iron oxide or pigmentary titanium dioxide can provide substantial high-energy visible light protection, which is why tinted mineral products are marketed for pigmentation-prone skin.[1] Wikipedia also notes that people tend to apply mineral sunscreens more thinly than chemical ones.[1]

Titanium dioxide appears in daily facial sunscreens, tinted moisturizers, mineral foundations and sunscreens for children and sensitive skin.[1][2] The appearance case for sunscreen rests on photoaging: Wikipedia's sunscreen article reports that a 2013 Australian study of about 900 light-skinned people found daily broad-spectrum use for 4.5 years left skin smoother and more resilient, and that a study of 32 subjects found daily SPF 30 use reversed photoaging within 12 weeks, with improvements lasting a year.[1] It also reports that sunscreen helps prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.[1] These findings concern sunscreens as a category rather than titanium dioxide specifically.

Mineral filters are often chosen by people who want to avoid specific organic filters, by those with reactive skin, and by those who want a tinted product that doubles as base makeup. The FDA notes that sunscreens that are not broad spectrum or are below SPF 15 must carry a warning that they help prevent sunburn but not skin cancer or early skin aging.[7]

Modern mineral sunscreens use ultrafine or nanoscale titanium dioxide, usually coated, because small particles scatter visible light less and so look more transparent on skin.[3][1] Unlike the EU, the US does not require labels to disclose mineral nanoparticles.[1]

Nanoscale anatase titanium dioxide can absorb UV and generate hydroxyl radicals, a property discovered by Akira Fujishima in 1967 and published in 1972 (the Honda-Fujishima effect) and later exploited in self-cleaning and antifogging coatings.[3] Sunscreen particles are generally coated, which is intended to limit this activity on skin.[3]

In the US the FDA began sorting UV filters in February 2019 into categories of generally recognized as safe and effective (GRASE), not GRASE because of safety concerns, and not GRASE pending more data; the 2021 order placed zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in the GRASE category, the only filters so classified. PABA and trolamine salicylate were reclassified as not GRASE and removed from the market.[1][7] GRASE status requires both animal and human clinical data.[1] The FDA has also requested more safety data on several organic filters after studies showed absorption into the bloodstream, though it has not said they are unsafe; those absorption studies concerned organic filters, not zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.[1][7]

In the EU, sunscreens are regulated as cosmetics under Regulation (EC) 1223/2009, labels must disclose nanoparticle ingredients, and zinc oxide was approved as a UV filter in 2016.[1] EU rules for the UVA seal require a UVA protection factor of at least one-third of the labelled SPF.[1]

Separately from sunscreen, titanium dioxide as the food colouring E171 was judged by the European Food Safety Authority in 2021 to be no longer safe as a food additive because genotoxicity could not be ruled out, and the EU withdrew its authorisation from 7 February 2022; the UK Food Standards Agency and Health Canada did not follow. This concerns ingestion, not topical sunscreen.[3]

A 1996 pilot study in Australia had patients scheduled for skin surgery apply microfine titanium dioxide sunscreen daily for 2 to 6 weeks beforehand and then analysed skin samples to assess percutaneous absorption, because the authors saw little prior data while the products were being widely recommended.[4]

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled titanium dioxide dust as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans; Wikipedia says this concerns inhaled dust rather than sunscreen use directly, and that IARC recommends against sprayable sunscreens because of inhalation risk.[3] Wikipedia also says it is not yet known how well healthy skin blocks absorption, or whether damaged skin or prolonged use raises exposure.[3] Public health bodies, as summarised on Wikipedia, generally judge the skin cancer risk from sun exposure to outweigh unproven concerns about approved filters.[1]

A 2019 study used Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast strains as a model to assess photoprotective and photomutagenic effects of a titanium dioxide sunscreen, reflecting a push for cell models that do not overestimate risks at unrealistic UV doses.[5]

Environmentally, Wikipedia says most nanoparticles from cosmetics enter wastewater and about 99 percent of them end up on land in sewage sludge rather than in water.[3] Advocates often recommend mineral sunscreens in place of oxybenzone and octinoxate products, which Hawaii banned in 2018, while a 2015 study found titanium dioxide nanoparticles under UV increased hydrogen peroxide production that can damage phytoplankton.[1] Labels such as reef-safe are not regulated.[1]

Titanium dioxide is usually paired with zinc oxide, whose powder blends are the subject of patents on particle-size mixtures designed to improve transparency and protection.[6][8] Other sun-protection measures that skin-care communities discuss alongside it include organic-filter sunscreens, shade, clothing and hats; the AAD guidance addresses sunscreen choice alongside shade and clothing.[2]

A 1996 pilot study in patients having skin surgery examined absorption of microfine titanium dioxide from sunscreen applied daily for 2 to 6 weeks.[4] No trials of appearance outcomes specific to titanium dioxide sunscreen were found; the photoaging trials above evaluated broad-spectrum sunscreen as a category.[1]

lore.intro: Mineral sunscreen is discussed in skincare circles as a gentler, non-chemical alternative to organic filters, with recurring arguments about white cast, nanoparticles and reef safety.
